newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU farm ministers meet to hear U.K. BSE report.
newsitem.headline: EU farm ministers meet to hear U.K. BSE report.

text.p: European Union farm ministers met on Monday to hear a report from Britain on progress it has made in fighting mad cow disease and fulfilling terms for lifting a worldwide ban on British beef.

EU leaders agreed in Florence in June a five-point plan for a phased lifting of the ban, imposed in March after the British government disclosed that the fatal disease, known as Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE), could spread to humans.
"We have made progress on four out of the five points," British agriculture minister Douglas Hogg told reporters as he entered the meeting.
Britain is introducing tighter animal feed, slaughter house and cattle processing controls as well as measures to identify and track animal movements.

But it says it is waiting for the advice of EU veterinary scientists about the fifth point -- a selective cull of up to 147,000 extra cattle most at risk to BSE -- after a British study claimed the disease could die out within five years.
The cull, which would supplement the annual slaughter of one million older animals over the age of 30 months.
After a slow start, Britain has speeded up the cull and has now slaughtered nearly 900,000 animals. It expects to have cleared the backlog by the end of the year.
This would allow the government, depending on the scientific advice and parliament's approval, to implement the extra cull.
Hogg said Britain would not present any proposal this week on exempting certified BSE-free herds from the ban but was continuing to discuss the idea with the European Commission.
"It is clearly desirable to get on with the problem of certified herds in a U.K.-wide way," he said.
Exemption of grass-fed herds, which could mainly benefit farmers in Northern Ireland where there is a computerised cattle tracking system, would be a first step in easing the global British ban.
But EU Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler has insisted that Britain must first carry out the extra cull.
